description: We're 3rd-year software engineering students from Curtin Colombo, Sri Lanka. Our strengths are Python, machine learning (PyTorch, scikit-learn, XGBoost), data analysis and FastAPI backends. We want to turn NASA's open data into something genuinely useful, and we aim to ship a working demo, not just slides.
summary:
SpaceShift is a web tool that turns SPHEREx images into a short video of any point in the sky, so anything that moves or changes brightness stands out.

SPHEREx maps the whole sky in 102 infrared colours, but each picture sees a given star at a different wavelength, so comparing pictures over time shows false flicker. SpaceShift fixes this in three steps. It compares only pictures taken at matching wavelengths. It moves each object to where it actually was on each picture's date, using its known motion. It lines up and adds faint exposures along that path. Users can also click any point for its spectrum and brightness over time, or compare the field with WISE images from 2010.

In real SPHEREx data, WISE 0855, the coldest known brown dwarf, is too faint to detect in one exposure (signal-to-noise 4.7), but clearly visible when 46 exposures are stacked (14). Our measurements agree with IRSA's own tool to about 2%.

Every view can be shared by link, so students and scientists alike can explore a changing sky without astronomy expertise.
details:
SpaceShift

A Time-Domain Exploration Platform for NASA's SPHEREx Mission

1. WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

SpaceShift takes any position in the sky (Right Ascension and Declination) or one of five predefined test targets and displays every available SPHEREx observation of that location over time. This allows users to identify objects that move or change in brightness.

SpaceShift is designed as a layered astronomical workbench with four primary capabilities.

1.1 Wavelength-Matched Blink and Difference Images

Each SPHEREx exposure captures a particular wavelength at a given position because the wavelength varies across the detector. Comparing exposures without accounting for this can make differences in colour appear to be actual changes in an object.

SpaceShift addresses this by:

  • Selecting only exposures where the wavelength at the target falls within a user-defined range.
  • Displaying selected exposures in chronological order as a blinking sequence.
  • Generating difference images by subtracting the first frame from subsequent observations.

This ensures that observed changes are more likely to represent genuine astronomical variations rather than differences in wavelength.

1.2 Motion-Tracked Stacking

Catalogue positions can become outdated, particularly for objects with high proper motion.

SpaceShift accounts for this by:

  • Using an object's known motion to calculate its predicted position at the date of each exposure.
  • Aligning individual exposures along the object's predicted trajectory.
  • Combining the aligned exposures to increase the signal-to-noise ratio.

This technique makes it possible to reveal faint moving objects that may not be detectable in individual exposures.

1.3 Click-to-Measure

Users can click on any point in the image to measure its brightness across all available exposures.

SpaceShift then generates:

  • Quick-Look Spectrum: Displays brightness measurements across different wavelengths.
  • Light Curve: Shows how an object's brightness changes over time.
  • Change Detection: Compares the average brightness between separate observation visits.

A change is reported only when the measured difference is at least five times the combined measurement error (5σ significance).

Users can also download the resulting measurements as a CSV file for further analysis.

1.4 Then and Now

SpaceShift provides a historical comparison by displaying the same region of the sky as observed by:

  • WISE: Historical observations from approximately 2010.
  • SPHEREx: More recent observations.

This allows users to visually compare the field across different survey periods and identify potential changes or moving objects.

2. WHAT WE CHECKED

We tested SpaceShift using real astronomical observations to evaluate its detection capabilities and measurement accuracy.

2.1 WISE 0855 Detection and Motion Validation

We tested the system using WISE 0855, the coldest known brown dwarf.

Our results demonstrated that:

  • A single exposure produced a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 4.7, below our detection threshold of 5.
  • Stacking 46 exposures along the object's predicted motion increased the SNR to 14.
  • The object's movement between observation visits closely followed its published proper motion predictions.

This demonstrates how motion-tracked stacking can reveal objects that are too faint to detect in individual exposures.

2.2 Measurement Accuracy

We also validated our measurement system against existing astronomical tools.

  • Quick-look measurements of a reference star agreed with NASA/IPAC IRSA's Spectrophotometry Tool to within approximately 2%.
  • WISE 0855 appeared approximately 1.4 arcseconds from its predicted position in the historical 2010 WISE image.

These checks provide evidence that our measurements and positional calculations are consistent with established astronomical references.

3. BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

SpaceShift aims to make astronomical time-domain exploration more accessible, interactive and efficient.

  • Accessibility: No formal astronomy training is required. Users can simply enter a sky position and explore the observations.
  • Shareability: Every view is represented by its web address, allowing students, teachers and researchers to share or embed specific observations.
  • Time-Domain Exploration: Unlike existing IRSA tools that primarily focus on precise spectral measurements of individual sources, SpaceShift focuses on identifying changes across entire sequences of observations.
  • Scalability: SPHEREx releases new datasets regularly. Supporting additional releases requires only a one-line configuration change.

4. TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

SpaceShift uses a modern, cross-platform technology stack combining astronomical data-processing libraries with web technologies.

4.1 Backend

Python, FastAPI, Astropy, PyVO and NumPy.

4.2 Frontend

React, TypeScript and Vite.

4.3 Sky Visualization

Aladin Lite (CDS).

4.4 Astronomical Data

SPHEREx DR1 and QR3, AllWISE.

4.5 Catalogue Sources

SIMBAD and Gaia DR3.

4.6 Data Infrastructure

NASA/IPAC IRSA and AWS Open Data.

4.7 Data Retrieval and Optimization

SpaceShift retrieves SPHEREx observations from NASA/IPAC's Infrared Science Archive (IRSA).

Rather than downloading complete 66 MB image files, the application accesses the AWS Open Data mirror of the archive and retrieves only the small image patches required for analysis.

Our performance tests demonstrated:

  • 258 image patches retrieved in approximately 75 seconds.
  • The standard cutout service takes approximately 12 seconds per cutout.

This significantly improves the efficiency of retrieving observations for interactive exploration.

4.8 Development Workflow

We also established a structured development workflow to support collaboration across the team.

  • GitHub for issue tracking, pull requests and automated testing.
  • An API contract generated directly from the backend code.
  • Mock data mode to allow frontend and backend development to proceed independently.
  • AI coding assistants to support selected implementation and documentation tasks, with their usage recorded in the repository.

The application runs entirely in a web browser and requires no specialised hardware.

5. WHAT MAKES SPACESHIFT CREATIVE?

Most astronomical tools treat individual SPHEREx images as spectral measurements. SpaceShift takes a different approach:

We treat the astronomical archive as a movie rather than a collection of independent images.

Our approach is built around two important ideas:

5.1 Compare Like with Like

By matching wavelengths across different exposures, SpaceShift minimises misleading visual differences caused by wavelength variations. This allows users to identify genuine changes in astronomical objects.

5.2 Follow Objects Through Time

Instead of stacking images at fixed sky coordinates, SpaceShift accounts for an object's motion and aligns observations along its predicted trajectory.

This allows faint moving objects to emerge from individual exposures that would otherwise be insufficient for detection.

Together, these techniques transform a large collection of astronomical observations into an interactive time-domain exploration experience.

6. FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Throughout development, we considered scientific accuracy, reliability, accessibility, openness and the practical realities of collaborative development.

6.1 Scientific Integrity

We prioritised transparency and scientific honesty.

  • Every reported numerical result can be traced to a documented validation check.
  • The interface clearly distinguishes between real astronomical data and demonstration data.
  • Saturated exposures are rejected rather than producing potentially misleading measurements.
  • The application warns users when another star falls within the measurement aperture.
  • Change detection verdicts are withheld when nearby sources could compromise measurement reliability.

6.2 Reliability

We designed the application to handle failures in external astronomical data services.

  • If the archive becomes unavailable or experiences an error, the application displays the last saved search and clearly communicates the issue.
  • Failed searches are never cached, preventing unsuccessful requests from being treated as valid results.

6.3 Accessibility

We aimed to make SpaceShift usable by people without specialised astronomical knowledge.

  • Keyboard-accessible controls.
  • Plain-language explanations for available options.
  • Interface layouts tested at laptop screen sizes.

6.4 Openness and Reproducibility

SpaceShift is designed to support transparency and further development.

  • Open-source code released under the Apache 2.0 licence.
  • Proper attribution for reused datasets and libraries.
  • Downloadable measurement results in CSV format.

6.5 Team and Development Constraints

Our team worked remotely using both Windows and macOS environments.

To accommodate these differences, we:

  • Used cross-platform development tools.
  • Maintained a consistent development workflow.
  • Used GitHub to coordinate contributions and track changes.
  • Regularly pushed and integrated code to minimise collaboration issues.

7. WHAT WE WOULD DO NEXT

Although SpaceShift already provides an interactive environment for exploring astronomical observations, several improvements could expand its capabilities and bring it closer to addressing the Planet X research question.

7.1 Automatic Source Detection

Currently, SpaceShift performs change detection only on locations selected by the user. The next step would be to scan the entire field automatically and flag every source that moves or changes in brightness.

Sources that do not match any known catalogue object would be labelled as "possible asteroid or artifact" rather than immediately being classified as a new planet. This would help avoid misleading scientific conclusions.

7.2 Searching for Unknown Moving Objects

The current motion-tracking system relies on published motion data to predict an object's position across different exposures.

To investigate objects whose motion is not yet known, we would extend this approach by testing multiple possible motion trajectories, stacking exposures along each trajectory and identifying locations where previously undetected faint objects emerge.

This would be an important step towards investigating the Planet X question.

7.3 Handling Bright and Crowded Stars

Currently, saturated stars are rejected, and the fitting process used to distinguish WISE 0855 from its neighbouring star is specifically configured for that target.

We would improve this by measuring bright stars using their unsaturated outer regions and incorporating Gaia positional data to distinguish closely spaced neighbouring sources across any field.

7.4 Improving Speed and Data Independence

A deep field that has not been previously viewed can take several minutes to load. Additionally, the application depends on the archive's search service to identify relevant observations.

Building our own index of which SPHEREx exposures cover each region of the sky would address both limitations by reducing search times and decreasing dependence on external archive services.

7.5 Searching by Object Name

Currently, only the five predefined test targets can be resolved by name.

Integrating a public astronomical name-resolution service such as SIMBAD would allow users to enter the name of any recognised astronomical object instead of manually providing its coordinates.

7.6 Growing with the SPHEREx Mission

As SPHEREx releases additional datasets, the number of available observations will increase.

Each new release would provide additional observation visits, allowing SpaceShift to produce deeper image stacks and longer light curves through a simple one-line configuration change.

CONCLUSION

SpaceShift transforms SPHEREx's extensive astronomical archive into an interactive time-domain exploration platform, making it easier to discover, investigate and understand objects that move or change over time.
